analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from erasing lawsuits against corporate executives and parent companies without their written consent.
analysis.headline: The bill had five Senate backers, including a member of the Judiciary chairman's own party, and it was referred to that committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a large company goes bankrupt, the bankruptcy court can currently wipe out lawsuits aimed not at the bankrupt company itself but at people around it — its officers, directors, employees, or corporate parent — as part of approving the reorganization plan. This bill would generally stop that: a bankruptcy judge could not release or modify a non-debtor's liability, or block a lawsuit against a non-debtor, unless that party expressly agreed in writing. It would also cap temporary injunctions pausing those lawsuits at 90 days in a Chapter 11 case, move appeals of such injunctions up to the federal courts of appeals, and let courts throw out a bankruptcy filed by a company that was created by a restructuring designed to split assets away from its liabilities in the previous ten years.
analysis.who_benefits: People with pending lawsuits against a company's officers, directors, employees, or corporate parent — for example victims of a drug, a defective product, or mass corporate misconduct — keep their right to sue even when a subsidiary files for bankruptcy. Under current law, courts in some parts of the country can extinguish those claims as part of confirming a reorganization plan, sometimes without the claimant's consent [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims suing executives and corporate parents

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a bankruptcy court from discharging, releasing, or modifying the liability of anyone other than the debtor — or enjoining lawsuits to enforce claims against them — except where that party gives express written consent, which cannot be inferred from silence or failure to object to a plan.
Caps a Chapter 11 bankruptcy court's temporary stay of a lawsuit against a non-debtor at 90 days, and makes the stay dissolve automatically unless a court of appeals affirms it in time.
Gives the federal courts of appeals, rather than district courts, jurisdiction over appeals of injunctions that pause lawsuits against non-debtors in Chapter 11 cases.

Requires dismissal of a Chapter 11 case, on request of a party in interest, if the debtor or its predecessor was created through a restructuring in the prior ten years that deliberately separated a company's assets from its liabilities while assigning the liabilities to the debtor.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate officers, directors, employees, and parent companies who would lose the ability to have their litigation liability erased in a subsidiary's bankruptcy; the bill would also make some complex reorganizations harder to settle because one of the tools courts used to broker global peace deals would be off the table unless every released party consents in writing [S2],[S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and parent companies facing lawsuits

drawbacks.text: The practice the bill bans is disputed even among courts — there is a split among the judicial circuits over whether bankruptcy courts can release non-debtor liability at all — and courts that allow it have often done so to carry out comprehensive settlements in which the released parties contributed money to compensate victims in exchange for peace. A blanket ban could make some global settlements harder or slower to reach, potentially leaving some claimants with less money and more years of litigation.

The bill preserves only narrow carve-outs — such as releases with express written consent, sales of estate property, and bar-date or indemnity-type claim administration — so genuine insolvency cases that relied on broad releases to bring every party to the table would need restructuring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims of corporate misconduct the bill closes a loophole through which people who never filed for bankruptcy could be shielded from their lawsuits as a side effect of someone else's reorganization. The honest trade-off is real: nondebtor releases have sometimes been the price that produced large settlement funds for victims quickly, and eliminating them in all cases could complicate those deals. The bill mitigates this by allowing consensual releases and by leaving most routine bankruptcy tools untouched, so the core reform — nobody's lawsuit is taken away without their knowing agreement — is well designed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was filed, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 28, 2021, for herself, Sen. Richard Durbin, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; that referral is the last action in the bill's history for the entire 117th Congress.
The bill drew four cosponsors — three Senate Democrats and one independent — and no Republicans.

The CRS summary notes that bankruptcy courts' power to release non-debtors from liability is contested, with a split among the judicial circuits on the practice, which is the problem the bill targets.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing mass lawsuits, their officers, directors, and parent companies, and the restructuring industry that brokers these deals — the court practice of releasing non-debtors from liability remained available because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies and executives facing mass-tort lawsuits

industries.industry: Corporate officers, directors, and parent companies facing mass-tort liability
industries.note: The bill removes their ability to have lawsuits brought by injured people — such as drug or product liability victims — extinguished in a bankruptcy they did not file, unless they agree in writing. Their interest lies in shedding that liability at victims' expense, which is exactly what the bill blocks.

industries.industry: Private equity and distressed-company restructuring dealmakers
industries.note: The bill lets courts dismiss a Chapter 11 case if the debtor was created by a restructuring that split assets from liabilities within the previous ten years, a move aimed at transactions that place liabilities in an underfunded shell while protected owners keep the valuable assets. Their business model relies on such structures remaining bankruptcy-proof.

Large mass-tort bankruptcies are among the most lucrative work in the field, and the ban on nondebtor releases plus the new dismissal power would reshape — and in some cases shrink — that practice, though complex litigation over the new rules would create work of its own. Their client base often wants releases, so their interest does not run with victims'.
